sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
> **Audience:** AI engineers with Python + LangChain + LangGraph foundation, ready to build a recruiter-ready portfolio.
> **Coverage:** Agentic AI · RAG + MCP · Security · Observability · Context Engineering · Fine-tuning (LoRA / QLoRA) · Local LLMs
> **Industries:** Generic IT · FinTech / Banking · E-commerce / SaaS
> **Format:** Deep-dive (~5 pages per project) with full runnable code, professional flowcharts, and end-to-end implementation guidance.

sections.title: Why This Guide Exists
sections.body:
Most AI engineers today know *how* to call an LLM, build a basic RAG chain, or fine-tune a model on a notebook. The gap between that level and being **hirable as a production Agentic AI engineer** is enormous. Hiring managers at IT firms in 2026 are not looking for someone who ran `ChatOpenAI().invoke("hello")` in a tutorial; they want engineers who can ship agents that are observable, secure, cost-controlled, and grounded in real business problems. This guide closes that gap by giving you 15 projects, each one tied to a real pain point that IT firms face right now — incident response, fraud, churn, code review, knowledge retrieval, support automation, and more.

Every project in this guide follows the same battle-tested structure: **real-world problem → tech stack → architecture → flowchart → full code → evaluation → deployment → portfolio narrative**. You can copy each project into a fresh GitHub repo, ship it in 2-3 weekends, and have a story to tell in interviews. The projects are sequenced from foundational (Project 1) to advanced (Project 15) so that skills compound — by Project 7 you will already be more capable than 80% of candidates applying for mid-level AI engineer roles. By Project 15, you will be doing on-device fine-tuning, MCP server design, and red-teaming — topics most engineers haven't even heard of.

The technologies you will touch span the entire modern Agentic AI stack: **LangGraph** for multi-agent orchestration, **LangChain** for chains and tool calls, **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** for standardized tool integration, **RAG** with vector + graph hybrid retrieval, **PEFT/QLoRA** for fine-tuning Llama and Mistral on consumer GPUs, **LangSmith + Arize Phoenix** for observability, **Guardrails AI + Garak** for security, and **context engineering** patterns for memory management at scale. After completing even 5 of these projects, you will have hands-on exposure to more production patterns than most bootcamps teach in 6 months.

sections.title: Recommended Learning Path (Build in This Order)
sections.body:
The projects are sequenced so that each new one builds on skills from the previous ones. If you are starting fresh, follow this path; if you already have some experience, you can jump to the relevant cluster.

### Phase A — Foundations (Weeks 1-3, Projects 1, 2, 5)

Start with single-agent orchestration patterns that mirror what real IT teams ship today. **Project 1 (Incident Response)** teaches you LangGraph's core primitives — `StateGraph`, conditional edges, `interrupt`, sub-agents — on a problem every IT firm deals with. **Project 2 (Code Review)** adds parallel agents and tool integration with GitHub APIs. **Project 5 (Self-Healing DevOps)** closes the loop by adding observability and feedback into the agent itself. After this phase, you will have 3 portfolio pieces that demonstrate multi-agent orchestration, tool use, and feedback loops — the foundation of every senior AI engineer's toolkit.

### Phase B — Retrieval & Memory (Weeks 4-6, Projects 3, 8, 10)

Move from "agent that acts" to "agent that knows." **Project 3 (Knowledge Graph RAG with MCP)** is the most important project in this guide for senior roles — it teaches hybrid retrieval (vector + graph), MCP server design, and multi-hop reasoning, all of which are 2026 hiring hot-spots. **Project 8 (Context Memory)** teaches context window engineering, summarization strategies, and long-term memory. **Project 10 (Multi-Modal RAG)** extends retrieval to images, a must-have skill for e-commerce and content-heavy applications. After Phase B, you can confidently architect production RAG systems that go far beyond naive `similarity_search()`.

### Phase C — Production Hardening (Weeks 7-9, Projects 6, 7, 11, 14)

Production agents die without security, observability, and cost control. **Project 6 (Secure RAG)** adds RBAC, PII detection, and prompt-injection defense. **Project 7 (Observability Platform)** teaches you to instrument every LLM call with tracing and automated hallucination detection — skills that map directly to "AI reliability engineer" roles. **Project 11 (Red-Teaming)** makes you think like an attacker, a rare skill that immediately differentiates you. **Project 14 (Multi-LLM Router)** teaches cost optimization, semantic caching, and eval-driven routing. After Phase C, you can ship agents that won't embarrass your employer.

### Phase D — Fine-tuning & Edge (Weeks 10-12, Projects 4, 9, 12, 13, 15)

The final phase covers skills most engineers never touch: streaming agents (**Project 4**), QLoRA fine-tuning (**Project 9**), real-time intervention agents (**Project 12**), MCP server design (**Project 13**), and on-device deployment (**Project 15**). These are the projects that get you past senior engineer screenings into staff / principal AI engineer conversations. They are also the projects most likely to be relevant in 2027 as the industry shifts from API-based LLM apps to fine-tuned, on-device, privacy-preserving agents.

sections.title: How Each Project Is Structured
sections.body:
Every project follows the same template so you can scan quickly and find what you need:

1. **Real-World Problem** — why IT firms care, with concrete numbers
2. **Tech Stack** — every tool, with version pins
3. **Architecture Overview** — text description of the system
4. **Solution Flowchart** — visual PNG showing the phased solution
5. **End-to-End Implementation** — full runnable Python code, broken into logical chunks with explanations
6. **Evaluation & Metrics** — how to know it works
7. **Deployment Notes** — Docker, CI/CD, scaling
8. **Common Pitfalls** — mistakes every engineer makes the first time
9. **Portfolio Highlights** — what to put on your GitHub README and resume

Code blocks are designed to be **copy-paste runnable**. Where a setup step is required (e.g., `pip install`, env vars), it's called out at the top of the code section. Where the code is too long for one block, it's split into logical files that mirror the actual repo structure you would create.

sections.title: Project 1: Multi-Agent IT Incident Response Pipeline
sections.body:
### Real-World Problem

Every mid-to-large IT firm loses millions annually to slow incident response. Industry studies (Ponemon 2024) put the average cost of a single IT incident at **$4,800/minute** of downtime, and the mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) at major SaaS firms is still **20-40 minutes** even with PagerDuty in place. The bottleneck is rarely detection — modern monitoring stacks (Datadog, Prometheus, Sentry) fire alerts within seconds. The bottleneck is **triage and diagnosis**: a human on-call engineer has to wake up, open a laptop, pull logs from 5 different tools, search Confluence for the runbook, check whether this incident happened before, and only then start fixing. This is exactly the kind of multi-step, tool-orchestrated, knowledge-grounded workflow that Agentic AI was built to automate.

A multi-agent incident response pipeline can compress MTTA from 30 minutes to under 5 minutes for known incident classes, and dramatically reduce the cognitive load on human engineers even for novel incidents by preparing a draft RCA, gathering relevant logs, and pre-filling the Slack incident channel. This project builds exactly that: a LangGraph-orchestrated system where specialist agents (Triage, Diagnostic, Remediation, Documentation) collaborate under a supervisor, with full observability and human-in-the-loop escalation for high-severity incidents.

### Tech Stack

| Component | Tool | Version |
|-----------|------|---------|
| Orchestration | LangGraph | 0.2.x |
| LLM | GPT-4o (supervisor), GPT-4o-mini (sub-agents) | Latest |
| Vector store | Qdrant (self-hosted) | 1.11.x |
| Embeddings | bge-large-en-v1.5 | 1.5 |
| Observability | LangSmith + Phoenix | Latest |
| Webhook server | FastAPI | 0.115 |
| Tools | kubectl, Terraform, Slack SDK, PyGithub | Latest |

### Architecture Overview

The system is a LangGraph `StateGraph` with a supervisor node and four specialist sub-agents. Alerts from Prometheus/Datadog/Sentry hit a FastAPI webhook endpoint, which normalizes the alert payload and writes it to the graph state. The supervisor inspects severity (P0-P3) and routes to the appropriate workflow. For P0/P1, the Triage Agent pulls recent logs and deploys, the Diagnostic Agent queries the runbook vector store for similar past incidents, and if similarity > 0.85, the Remediation Agent replays the historical fix (kubectl rollout, Terraform apply) under a sandboxed service account. For novel incidents, the supervisor calls `interrupt()` to page a human, while the Documentation Agent drafts a Slack summary and a Confluence postmortem template. The Validation Agent re-runs health checks after any remediation and either closes the incident or escalates. Every node is traced in LangSmith and Phoenix for post-incident audit.

### Solution Flowchart

![Project 1 Flowchart](flowcharts/flowchart_01.png)

### End-to-End Implementation

#### Step 1 — Environment Setup

```bash
mkdir incident-agent && cd incident-agent
python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install langgraph langchain langchain-openai \
            fastapi uvicorn qdrant-client sentence-transformers \
            slack-sdk PyGithub phoenix opentelemetry-sdk \
            langfuse
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
export SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-...
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...
export LANGSMITH_API_KEY=ls__...
export LANGSMITH_PROJECT=incident-agent
```

#### Step 2 — State & Tool Definitions (`state.py`)

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal, Annotated
from langgraph.graph import MessagesState, add_messages
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum

class Severity(str, Enum):
    P0 = "P0"  # total outage
    P1 = "P1"  # major degradation
    P2 = "P2"  # minor degradation
    P3 = "P3"  # cosmetic

class Incident(BaseModel):
    incident_id: str
    source: str  # "prometheus" | "datadog" | "sentry" | "manual"
    severity: Severity
    service: str
    summary: str
    fired_at: datetime
    raw_alert: dict
    similar_incidents: list[dict] = Field(default_factory=list)
    proposed_fix: str | None = None
    applied_fix: str | None = None
    status: Literal["open", "diagnosing", "fixing", "verifying", "resolved", "escalated"] = "open"
    human_required: bool = False

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    incident: Incident
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]
    tool_outputs: dict
    trace_id: str
```

#### Step 3 — Tool Definitions (`tools.py`)

```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from kubernetes import client, config
import subprocess, json
from slack_sdk import WebClient
import os

# Load kube config once at import time
try:
    config.load_kube_config()
    k8s = client.AppsV1Api()
except Exception:
    k8s = None  # running outside cluster

slack = WebClient(token=os.environ["SLACK_BOT_TOKEN"])

@tool
def get_pod_logs(service: str, namespace: str = "default", tail_lines: int = 200) -> str:
    """Fetch last N log lines from a Kubernetes service's pods."""
    if not k8s:
        return f"[mock] logs for {service}/{namespace}"
    pods = k8s.list_namespaced_pod(namespace, label_selector=f"app={service}")
    if not pods.items:
        return f"No pods found for service={service}"
    logs = []
    for pod in pods.items[:3]:  # cap at 3 pods
        try:
            log = k8s.read_namespaced_pod_log(pod.metadata.name, namespace, tail_lines=tail_lines)
            logs.append(f"--- {pod.metadata.name} ---\n{log}")
        except Exception as e:
            logs.append(f"Error reading {pod.metadata.name}: {e}")
    return "\n".join(logs)

@tool
def restart_deployment(service: str, namespace: str = "default") -> str:
    """Restart a Kubernetes deployment by patching the restart annotation."""
    if not k8s:
        return f"[mock] would restart {service}"
    body = {"spec": {"template": {"metadata": {"annotations": {"kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt": "now"}}}}}
    k8s.patch_namespaced_deployment(service, namespace, body)
    return f"Restarted deployment {service}/{namespace}"

@tool
def query_runbook_store(query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    """Search past incident runbooks in Qdrant by semantic similarity."""
    from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    qc = QdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
    enc = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5")
    vec = enc.encode(query).tolist()
    hits = qc.query_points("runbooks", query=vec, limit=top_k).points
    return [{"score": h.score, "text": h.payload["text"], "incident_id": h.payload.get("incident_id")} for h in hits]

@tool
def post_to_slack(channel: str, message: str) -> str:
    """Post a message to a Slack channel."""
    resp = slack.chat_postMessage(channel=channel, text=message)
    return f"Posted to {channel}, ts={resp['ts']}"

@tool
def run_command(cmd: str, timeout: int = 30) -> str:
    """Run a shell command (sandboxed). Use for terraform apply, etc."""
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
        return f"EXIT={r.returncode}\nSTDOUT={r.stdout[:2000]}\nSTDERR={r.stderr[:2000]}"
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return f"TIMEOUT after {timeout}s"
```

#### Step 4 — Agent Nodes (`agents.py`)

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from state import AgentState, Incident, Severity
from tools import get_pod_logs, restart_deployment, query_runbook_store, post_to_slack, run_command

llm_big = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)
llm_small = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)

# --- Triage Agent ---
def triage_node(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    logs = get_pod_logs.invoke({"service": inc.service})
    runbooks = query_runbook_store.invoke({"query": f"{inc.summary} {inc.service} {inc.severity}"})
    inc.similar_incidents = runbooks
    msg = llm_small.invoke([
        SystemMessage(content="You are an incident triage agent. Given logs and similar past incidents, "
                              "produce a 3-bullet diagnosis. Be terse, factual, no fluff."),
        HumanMessage(content=f"INCIDENT:\n{inc.summary}\n\nLOGS:\n{logs[:3000]}\n\n"
                              f"SIMILAR PAST INCIDENTS:\n{runbooks}")
    ])
    return {"incident": inc, "messages": [msg]}

# --- Diagnostic Agent ---
def diagnostic_node(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    top_sim = max(inc.similar_incidents, key=lambda x: x["score"]) if inc.similar_incidents else None
    if top_sim and top_sim["score"] > 0.85:
        inc.proposed_fix = top_sim["text"]
        return {"incident": inc, "messages": [HumanMessage(content=f"High-similarity match found: {top_sim}"),
                                              HumanMessage(content=f"Proposed fix (from past incident): {top_sim['text']}")]}
    # Novel incident: draft RCA for human
    inc.human_required = True
    rca = llm_big.invoke([
        SystemMessage(content="You are an SRE principal. Draft a root-cause hypothesis + 3 next-step "
                              "investigations for the on-call engineer. Cite log evidence."),
        HumanMessage(content=f"Summary: {inc.summary}\nLogs excerpt: {state['messages'][-1].content[:2000]}")
    ])
    post_to_slack.invoke({"channel": "#incidents", "message": f":rotating_light: *{inc.incident_id}* needs human. RCA draft:\n{rca.content}"})
    return {"incident": inc, "messages": [rca]}

# --- Remediation Agent ---
def remediation_node(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    if not inc.proposed_fix:
        return {"messages": [HumanMessage(content="No proposed fix; skipping remediation.")]}
    # For demo: only allow kubectl restart; in prod, parse proposed_fix for the right tool
    result = restart_deployment.invoke({"service": inc.service})
    inc.applied_fix = result
    inc.status = "verifying"
    return {"incident": inc, "messages": [HumanMessage(content=f"Remediation applied: {result}")]}

# --- Validation Agent ---
def validation_node(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    # In prod: hit health endpoint, check error rate, etc.
    health = run_command.invoke({"cmd": f"curl -sf http://{inc.service}/health || echo DOWN"})
    if "DOWN" in health:
        inc.status = "escalated"
        post_to_slack.invoke({"channel": "#incidents", "message": f":x: {inc.incident_id} still DOWN after fix. Escalating."})
    else:
        inc.status = "resolved"
        post_to_slack.invoke({"channel": "#incidents", "message": f":white_check_mark: {inc.incident_id} RESOLVED."})
    return {"incident": inc}

# --- Supervisor router ---
def supervisor_router(state: AgentState) -> str:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    if inc.human_required:
        return "validation"  # skip remediation, go straight to verify
    if inc.proposed_fix:
        return "remediation"
    return "diagnostic"

def entry_router(state: AgentState) -> str:
    inc: Incident = state["incident"]
    if inc.severity in (Severity.P0, Severity.P1):
        return "triage"
    return "triage"  # could route P3 directly to docs
```

#### Step 5 — Graph Assembly (`graph.py`)

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from state import AgentState
from agents import (triage_node, diagnostic_node, remediation_node,
                    validation_node, supervisor_router, entry_router)

builder = StateGraph(AgentState)
builder.add_node("triage", triage_node)
builder.add_node("diagnostic", diagnostic_node)
builder.add_node("remediation", remediation_node)
builder.add_node("validation", validation_node)

builder.set_entry_point("triage")
builder.add_conditional_edges("triage", entry_router, {"triage": "diagnostic"})
builder.add_conditional_edges("diagnostic", supervisor_router,
                              {"remediation": "remediation", "validation": "validation"})
builder.add_edge("remediation", "validation")
builder.add_edge("validation", END)

memory = MemorySaver()
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=memory, interrupt_before=["remediation"])  # human-in-loop gate
```

#### Step 6 — FastAPI Webhook (`api.py`)

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks
from pydantic import BaseModel
from datetime import datetime
import uuid, json
from state import Incident, Severity
from graph import graph

app = FastAPI()

class AlertIn(BaseModel):
    source: str
    severity: str
    service: str
    summary: str
    raw: dict

@app.post("/alert")
async def receive_alert(alert: AlertIn, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    inc = Incident(
        incident_id=f"INC-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        source=alert.source,
        severity=Severity(alert.severity),
        service=alert.service,
        summary=alert.summary,
        fired_at=datetime.utcnow(),
        raw_alert=alert.raw,
    )
    bg.add_task(run_graph, inc)
    return {"incident_id": inc.incident_id, "status": "accepted"}

def run_graph(inc: Incident):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": inc.incident_id}}
    state = {"incident": inc, "messages": [], "tool_outputs": {}, "trace_id": inc.incident_id}
    for event in graph.stream(state, config=config):
        print(json.dumps({k: str(v)[:200] for k, v in event.items()}, default=str))
```

#### Step 7 — Run It

```bash

docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant
python ingest_runbooks.py  # see repo

# Terminal 2: API server
uvicorn api:app --reload --port 8000

# Terminal 3: simulate alert
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/alert -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "source": "prometheus",
  "severity": "P1",
  "service": "checkout-api",
  "summary": "checkout-api 5xx error rate > 10% for 3 min",
  "raw": {"alertname": "HighErrorRate", "fired_at": "2026-01-15T10:30:00Z"}
}'
```

### Evaluation & Metrics

| Metric | Target | How to Measure |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| MTTA (acknowledge) | < 30s | Webhook receive → first Slack post |
| MTTR (resolve, known incidents) | < 5 min | Webhook → `status=resolved` |
| False-positive fix rate | < 5% | Audit remediation actions per week |
| Escalation accuracy | > 90% | Human reviews each escalation; should agree it needed human |
| Runbook retrieval relevance | Top-1 score > 0.7 | LangSmith eval set |

Set up a **golden set** of 30 historical incidents with known fixes. Run them through the pipeline nightly; track fix-rate and false-positive rate over time as a regression dashboard in Phoenix.

### Deployment Notes

Containerize the FastAPI app + graph with Docker. Use **Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler** because LangGraph streaming is stateful — each pod handles a fixed shard of incidents by hashing `incident_id`. Persist Qdrant as a `StatefulSet`. Store LangSmith traces to a dedicated project per environment (`incident-agent-dev`, `incident-agent-prod`). The `interrupt_before=["remediation"]` gate means P0/P1 incidents wait for human approval before any `kubectl` action — critical for production trust. For P2/P3, you can remove the gate and let the agent auto-remediate.

### Common Pitfalls

1. **Trusting similarity scores blindly** — a 0.86 cosine match can still be a different root cause. Always include the past incident's resolution *and* its failure mode in the prompt so the LLM can sanity-check.
2. **Letting the agent run any shell command** — `run_command` is dangerous. In production, allowlist commands (Terraform plans from a vetted module registry) and run them in a sidecar with read-only RBAC where possible.
3. **Forgetting to dedupe alerts** — Prometheus fires the same alert every 30s during an outage. Your webhook must dedupe by `(alertname, service, fingerprint)` within a 5-minute window or you'll have 20 graphs running for one incident.
4. **Not testing the rollback path** — if the agent's fix makes things worse, you need a fast rollback. Always snapshot pre-fix state (e.g., previous Deployment manifest) so a human can revert in one command.

### Portfolio Highlights

- **README headline:** "Reduced incident MTTR by 80% for known incident classes using a 4-agent LangGraph pipeline with human-in-the-loop escalation"
- **Architecture diagram:** include the flowchart PNG
- **Demo GIF:** simulate a P1 alert, show Slack messages arriving in real time
- **Blog post:** write a 1500-word Medium post on "Patterns for human-in-the-loop in LangGraph"
- **Resume bullet:** "Built multi-agent incident response system handling 200+ alerts/month, auto-resolving 60%, reducing on-call engineer wake-ups by 70%"
